cells.tense: You know what you're holding up, and you're holding it with your eyes open.
cells.ask: Today, say out loud to one person one thing you can see clearly about a choice in front of you — before you've worked out what to do about it. Saying it where someone can hear puts it somewhere it can't drift.
cells.core:
When this part of you is working well, you take the weight and you don't go stiff doing it. You keep your grip and your openness at once — you can name what you're carrying, you can still be talked to while you carry it, and you're not bracing against the next thing before it arrives.

What you see, you see whole, and you don't wait for the last piece to land before you let yourself know it. The thing in your arms is exactly as heavy as it is, and none of your energy goes into pretending otherwise. There's one piece of it nobody has heard yet. Handing that over is the next small move.
cells.sheetLine: You carry what's heavy and you don't look away from it.
cells.handle: …there's one piece of it nobody has heard yet.
cells.verb: to see the whole thing and stop hunting for what's hidden

cells.tense: You've run this all the way to its ending and it hasn't started yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you feel sure about how it turns out. Today, make one small move on it before you've finished understanding it — a step you'd normally wait on. Coming in without the ending pre-written gives you something certainty can't.
cells.core:
When this part of you is working well, you hold what needs holding here in the present. You deal with what's actually in front of you and you find out what it's made of by picking it up — not by running the whole thing to its end in advance.

The ending got written before the thing started. You know how the conversation goes, where the project lands, what they'll say — and you're braced for a scene that hasn't happened. The read is real; the timing isn't. You're carrying weight from a future nobody handed you, and the part you could actually put your hands on keeps going by.

cells.tense: You stopped looking years back and you've been carrying blind since.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you're actually holding right now — one line, on paper, where you can see it. Naming what's in your arms from the outside gives you back the say over what you put down.
cells.core:
When this part of you is working well, you name the thing before you pick it up. You look at it first, decide whether it's yours, and set an edge around what you'll take on — which is how you can keep carrying it for as long as it needs carrying.

At some point, looking got too expensive. If you saw clearly what was going into your arms, you'd have had to set some of it down, so the looking stopped — and you kept taking things in. You know the weight. You can't say what it is. A load you can't name is one you can't finish, because you didn't agree to pick it up in the first place.

cells.handle: …a load you can't name is one you can't finish.

cells.tense: You can see the shape of this already, and you talk like it's still coming into view.
cells.ask: Name one thing you can see clearly and have been calling 'not my call' or 'still forming' — say it once as your own read, to yourself or to one person. Claiming what you see puts it back in your hands.
cells.core:
When this part of you is working well, the full picture is yours and you stand in it. You say what you see and you let it be what it is — no inflating it, no apologizing for it. You hold what's heavy and you don't have to prove you're strong to keep holding on.

The read happened a while back and the owning hasn't caught up. You can describe how this is, plainly, in the same breath as calling it something you're still gathering information about — someone else's decision, a situation still developing. Nothing is hidden from you. The one step left is saying that the clear thing is yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claims are the specific pictures I give for Fortitude going well — I inferred 'carrying without hardening and without building a shell around it' from the seat's own definition, which is fair, but 'you carry it and stay open' is the reading, not the record; a reader might say their carrying looks like refusing help, not holding steady. The asks all survive being wrong because none requires the person to agree with my read — they're small doable acts, and each teaches something regardless. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any 'you already…' opening that wants credit for seeing; I've kept the Unacknowledged cell locating rather than praising its own insight.
